title: Respiratory Failure and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: Which thresholds define respiratory failure on page 230?
opts: Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 90%; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on room air
Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg on oxygen; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on oxygen
Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 80 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 90%; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 45 mmHg on room air
Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 80%; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on room air
questions.exp: The definition box reads 'Hypoxemic : PaO2 <60 mmHg on room air, SpO2 <90%' and 'Hypercapnic : PaCO2 >50 mmHg on room air'. Both thresholds are specified on room air. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: Match each abbreviation in the page 230 box with its printed meaning — 1) PAO2 2) PaO2 3) PaCO2 4) PAO2 − PaO2 … A) Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in artery (normal ~40 mmHg) B) Partial pressure of oxygen in alveoli C) Alveolocapillary oxygen gradient D) Partial pressure of oxygen in artery (normal ~97 mmHg)
questions.exp: The box reads 'PAO2 : Partial pressure of oxygen in alveoli', 'PaO2 : Partial pressure of oxygen in artery (Normal ~97mmHg)', 'PaCO2 : Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in artery (Normal ~40mmHg)' and 'PAO2 − PaO2 : Alveolocapillary oxygen gradient'. The capital-A subscript is alveolar and the lower-case-a subscript arterial. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: Which pathology chain is printed in the Type I column on page 230?
opts: Impaired diffusion → ventilatory failure, with the low (15 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia
Impaired diffusion → oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia
Hypoventilation → oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and hypercapnia
Impaired perfusion → oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia
questions.exp: The Type I pathology cell reads 'Impaired diffusion → Oxygenation failure', then 'High (150 times) diffusion potential of CO' and 'No hypercapnia', with an alveolus-capillary diagram beneath. The 150-fold figure explains why CO transfer is used to measure diffusion. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: Which set of partial pressures belongs to Type I respiratory failure on page 230?
opts: ↓PaO2, ↑PaCO2, normal PAO2 − PaO2
Normal PaO2, ↓PaCO2, ↑PAO2 − PaO2
↓PaO2, normal PaCO2, ↑PAO2 − PaO2
↓PaO2, ↑PaCO2, ↑PAO2 − PaO2
questions.exp: The partial-pressure column of Type I reads '↓PaO2', 'Normal PaCO2' and '↑PAO2 − PaO2'. A raised CO2 with a normal gradient is the Type II pattern, and a raised CO2 with a raised gradient the Type III pattern, both on the next page. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: Which aetiological groups are listed in the Type I column besides ILD, pulmonary oedema/ARDS and pneumonia?
opts: Emphysema (↓surface area/volume), vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis
Emphysema (↑surface area/volume), vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis
Emphysema (↓surface area/volume), vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis
Pleural effusion, vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis
questions.exp: The Type I aetiology cell reads 'Fibrosis of interstitium : ILD', 'Fluid in interstitium, Pulmonary edema, ARDS', 'Exudate, Consolidation (Pneumonia)', 'Impaired alveolocapillary membrane unit ↓ surface area : Emphysema volume', then vascular causes, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: Bronchial asthma appears as a special Type I entry with a bracketed explanation. Which statements are printed?
opts: Airway disease with normal parenchyma → absent CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↑DLCO (normal diffusion)
Interstitial disease with normal airways → absent CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↑DLCO
Airway disease with normal parenchyma → absent CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↓DLCO (impaired diffusion)
Airway disease with abnormal parenchyma → present CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with ↑PaCO2 but ↓DLCO
questions.exp: The asthma entry reads 'Airway disease (Normal parenchyma, → Absent CO2 retention)' and '↓PaO2, (N) PaCO2, ↑DLCO (normal diffusion)'. Because the alveolo-capillary membrane is spared, diffusion is preserved and CO2 is not retained. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the Type I definition printed on page 230.
opts: False — Type I failure is a ventilatory failure with a raised PaCO2
False — the CO diffusion potential is quoted as 15 times on this page
True — Type I failure always requires a raised PAO2 − PaO2 with a raised PaCO2
True — Type I failure is an oxygenation failure with a normal PaCO2, and the CO diffusion potential is quoted as 150 times
questions.exp: The Type I column reads 'Oxygenation failure', 'No hypercapnia' and 'High (150 times) diffusion potential of CO', with 'Normal PaCO2' in the pressure column. A raised CO2 would make it Type II or III. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
questions.q: A patient with severe asthma has PaO2 55 mmHg, a normal PaCO2 and normal diffusion. Using the page 230 asthma entry, why is CO2 not retained?
opts: Airway disease with abnormal parenchyma means present CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with ↑PaCO2 and ↓DLCO
Airway disease with normal parenchyma means absent CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with (N)PaCO2 and ↑DLCO
Interstitial disease with normal airways means absent CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with (N)PaCO2 and ↓DLCO
Airway disease with normal parenchyma means present CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with ↑PaCO2 and ↑DLCO
questions.exp: The asthma rows read 'Airway disease (Normal parenchyma, → Absent CO2 retention)' and '↓PaO2, (N)PaCO2, ↑DLCO (normal diffusion)'. Because the alveolo-capillary membrane is intact, CO2 diffuses freely and the DLCO is preserved. (Book p230)

questions.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
questions.q: Which Type III chain and aetiology pair are printed on page 231?
opts: Oxygenation failure → parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure, with ILD acting through ↓compliance and ARDS through ↓diffusion
Hypoventilation → parenchymal damage → oxygenation failure, with ILD acting through ↓compliance and ARDS through ↓diffusion
Ventilatory failure → parenchymal damage → oxygenation failure, with ILD acting through ↓diffusion and ARDS through ↑lung compliance
Oxygenation failure → parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure, with ILD acting through ↓diffusion and ARDS through ↓lung compliance
questions.exp: The Type III row reads 'Oxygenation failure → Parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure', and the aetiology cell brackets 'ILD : ↓Diffusion' and 'ARDS : ↓Lung compliance' to 'Type 1 → Type 3 as disease progresses'. Type III therefore carries both a low PaO2 and a high PaCO2 with a raised gradient. (Book p231)

questions.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
questions.q: Which Type IV mechanism and causes are printed on page 231?
opts: Hypotension → ↓diffusion across the membrane, with cardiogenic, hypovolemic and septic shock as causes
Hypotension → ↓perfusion of respiratory muscles, with cardiogenic, hypovolemic and septic shock as causes
Hypotension → ↓perfusion of respiratory muscles, with obstructive, neurogenic and anaphylactic shock as causes
Hypertension → ↑perfusion of respiratory muscles, with cardiogenic, hypovolemic and septic shock as causes
questions.exp: The Type IV row reads 'Hypotension → ↓Perfusion of respiratory muscles' with the partial-pressure cell printed as a dash, and aetiology 'Cardiogenic shock, Hypovolemic shock, Septic shock'. The failure is of the respiratory pump, so pressures are not characteristic. (Book p231)

questions.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
questions.q: The 'Type-3 respiratory failure' note on page 231 is set in anaesthesiology. Which mechanism is printed?
opts: ↓Functional residual capacity (tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op atelectasis)
↓Vital capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op pneumonia)
↓Functional residual capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op atelectasis)
↑Functional residual capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op atelectasis)
questions.exp: The note reads 'Type-3 Respiratory Failure : in Anesthesiology' with 'Pathology : ↓ Functional Residual Capacity (Residual Volume + Expiratory Reserve Volume)' leading to 'Collapse (Post op Atelectasis)'. Note the page uses 'Type-3' here for a perioperative mechanism distinct from the Type III parenchymal row above it (recorded in the caveat file). (Book p231)

questions.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
questions.q: Which four causes of the anaesthesiology type-3 failure are printed?
opts: Supine position/obese/ascites, residual effects of anaesthesia, upper abdominal incision and airway secretions
Supine position/cachexia/ascites, muscle relaxants, upper abdominal incision and airway secretions
Supine position/obese/ascites, residual effects of anaesthesia, upper abdominal incision and pulmonary embolism
Prone position/obese/ascites, residual effects of anaesthesia, lower abdominal incision and airway secretions
questions.exp: The aetiology list reads 'supine position, Obese, Ascites', 'Residual effects of Anesthesia', 'upper abdominal incision' and 'Airway secretions'. All four reduce FRC or impede its restoration after surgery. (Book p231)

questions.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
questions.q: Which V/Q ratio values are printed under the hypoxemic-failure clinical approach?
opts: Normal 1.0; upper zone > 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q); lower zone < 1 (dependent area)
Normal 0.8; upper zone > 1 (dependent area); lower zone < 1 (non-dependent area)
Normal 0.8; upper zone < 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q); lower zone > 1 (dependent area)
Normal 0.8; upper zone > 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q); lower zone < 1 (dependent area)
questions.exp: The page prints 'Normal : 0.8', 'upper zone : >1 (Non-dependent area → ↓↓V, ↓↓Q)' and 'Lower zone : <1 (Dependent area)', adding that the ratio 'Indicates overall respiratory functional status of lung' and plays a role in type 1 failure. (Book p231)

questions.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
questions.q: Match each physiology with its printed row in the ventilation table — 1) Dead space physiology 2) Shunt physiology 3) Normal matching … A) Ventilation absent, perfusion present, V/Q zero B) V/Q 0.8 C) Ventilation present, perfusion absent, V/Q infinite
questions.exp: The table reads: dead space — ventilation present, perfusion absent, V/Q ∞, aetiology pulmonary embolism and pulmonary vascular disease; shunt — ventilation absent, perfusion present, V/Q zero, aetiology intracardiac/vascular shunts. Normal matching carries the V/Q of 0.8 printed above the table. (Book p231)

questions.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the Type III and Type IV rows on page 231.
opts: True — Type III has ↓PaO2 with ↑PaCO2 and ↑PAO2 − PaO2, while the Type IV partial-pressure cell is printed as a dash
True — Type IV is caused by parenchymal damage rather than by shock
False — Type IV is printed with a full set of partial pressures
False — Type III has ↓PaO2 with normal PaCO2 and a normal gradient
questions.exp: The Type III pressure cell reads '↓PaO2, ↑PaCO2, ↑PAO2 − PaO2', whereas the Type IV cell contains only a dash, consistent with a perfusion failure of the respiratory muscles rather than a gas-exchange defect. (Book p231)

questions.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
questions.q: The hypoxemic-failure flowchart begins with ↓PaO2 and three first-level branches. Which three are printed?
opts: Diffusion abnormality (Type III), V/Q = 0 shunt and V/Q = ∞ dead space
V/Q mismatch (Type I respiratory failure, diffusion abnormality), V/Q = 0 shunt and V/Q = ∞ dead space
V/Q mismatch (Type I respiratory failure, diffusion abnormality), V/Q = 0 dead space and V/Q = ∞ shunt
V/Q mismatch (Type II respiratory failure), V/Q = 1 shunt and V/Q = 0 dead space
questions.exp: The three arrows from ↓PaO2 read 'V/Q mismatch : Type-I respiratory failure (Diffusion abnormality)', 'V/Q = 0 Shunt' and 'V/Q = ∞ Dead space'. The shunt and dead space branches reproduce page 209's definitions exactly. (Book p232)

questions.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
questions.q: Match each flowchart terminal with its printed label — 1) Raised CO2 with a normal gradient 2) Raised CO2 with a raised gradient 3) Normal CO2 with a raised gradient not corrected by oxygen 4) Normal CO2 with a normal gradient … A) Shunt B) Hypoventilation (Type II) C) High altitude D) Hypoventilation plus another mechanism (Type III)
questions.exp: The chart prints 'Hypoventilation (Type II)', 'Hypoventilation + Another mechanism (Type III)', then under Type I the oxygen-response test ends at 'v/Q : mismatch' (corrects) or 'Shunt' (does not correct), and 'High Altitude' sits on the branch with no gradient. (Book p232)

questions.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
questions.q: According to the page 232 flowchart, how is a Type I hypoxaemia separated into V/Q mismatch versus shunt?
opts: Give oxygen: if the low PaO2 is corrected it is V/Q mismatch; if it is not corrected it is shunt
Measure the A-a gradient: if raised it is shunt; if normal it is V/Q mismatch
Give oxygen: if the low PaO2 is corrected it is shunt; if it is not corrected it is V/Q mismatch
Measure the PaCO2: if raised it is shunt; if normal it is V/Q mismatch
questions.exp: The Type I branch runs 'Low PO2 Corrected with O2 → Yes → v/Q : mismatch' and '→ No → Shunt'. Shunted blood never contacts ventilated alveoli, so added oxygen cannot reach it. (Book p232)

questions.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
questions.q: On the page 232 flowchart, a low PaO2 with a normal gradient and no CO2 retention leads to the terminal labelled ______.
opts: Dead space
High altitude
Hypoventilation
Shunt
questions.exp: The far-right branch of the Type I limb ends at 'High Altitude'. There the inspired oxygen pressure itself is low, so the gradient stays normal — unlike shunt or V/Q mismatch. (Book p232)

questions.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
questions.q: The hypercapnic-failure flowchart at the foot of page 232 begins with ↑PaCO2 and splits on the A-a gradient. Which two terminals are printed?
opts: Increased gradient → hypoventilation → generator, pumps, effector organ; normal gradient → V/Q mismatch, eg ARDS and ILD
Normal gradient → hypoventilation → generator and pumps only; increased gradient → diffusion defect, eg pulmonary embolism
Normal gradient → hypoventilation → generator, pumps, effector organ; increased gradient → V/Q mismatch, eg ARDS and ILD
Normal gradient → shunt; increased gradient → dead space, eg ARDS and ILD
questions.exp: The chart reads '↑PaCO2 → PAO2 − PaO2', then 'Normal → Hypoventilation → Generator, Pumps, Effector organ' and 'Increased → v/Q mismatch eg : ARDS ILD'. The generator/pump/effector trio matches the Type II aetiology list on page 230. (Book p232)

questions.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
questions.q: A patient has PaO2 50 mmHg, a normal PaCO2 and a raised A-a gradient; the PaO2 does not improve on 100% oxygen. Where does the page 232 algorithm place this?
opts: Type I respiratory failure with a shunt
Type II respiratory failure from hypoventilation
Type I respiratory failure with V/Q mismatch
Type III respiratory failure with a high altitude mechanism
questions.exp: The Type I limb splits on oxygen responsiveness: corrected PaO2 means V/Q mismatch, uncorrected means 'Shunt'. A normal PaCO2 keeps the case out of the Type II and III Hypoventilation terminals. (Book p232)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: Which synonyms for ARDS are printed at the top of page 233?
opts: Shock lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute interstitial pneumonia
Shock lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury
Shock lung, chronic lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury
Stiff lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury
questions.exp: The line reads 'AKA shock lung/acute lung injury/DAD/blast lung/acute alveolar injury.' Acute interstitial pneumonia is a separate idiopathic interstitial pneumonia listed on page 236, not a synonym for ARDS. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: Which three 1992 AECC criteria carry numbers on page 233?
opts: PCWP > 18 mmHg, bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200
PCWP < 18 mmHg, unilateral alveolar infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 300
PCWP < 18 mmHg (measuring left atrial pressure), bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200
PCWP < 15 mmHg, bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200
questions.exp: The AECC block reads 'Non cardiogenic pulmonary edema' with 'PCWP : <18 mm Hg (Suggestive of no cardiac abnormality)', then 'Bilateral alveolar and interstitial lung infiltrates on x-ray' and 'PaO2/FiO2 < 200'. The wedge pressure must be low, confirming a non-cardiogenic cause. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: What limitation and mortality figures are printed for ARDS on page 233?
opts: Only 20% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 30–40% with post-ARDS residual disability
Only 20% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 70–75% with no residual disability
Only 50% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 70–75% with post-ARDS residual disability
Only 20% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 70–75% with post-ARDS residual disability
questions.exp: The limitations line reads 'Only 20% patients meet ARDS criteria', and the note gives 'mortality : 70–75%' plus 'Post ARDS residual disability present'. Survivors are left with functional impairment, not a full recovery. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: Which four Berlin 2012 criteria are numbered on page 233?
opts: Acute onset within 1 month of the insult, bilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, non-cardiogenic with a normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O
Acute onset within 1 week of the insult, unilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, cardiogenic with an abnormal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 10 cm of H2O
Acute onset within 1 week of the insult, bilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, non-cardiogenic with a normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O
Acute onset within 1 week of the insult, bilateral infiltrates, non-cardiogenic with a normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured on room air without PEEP
questions.exp: The Berlin block reads '1. Acute onset : within 1 week of clinical insult/worsening respiratory symptoms', '2. Chest x-ray : Bilateral alveolar/Interstitial infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules', '3. Non cardiogenic : Normal ECHO' and '4. Oxygenation :' with the brace 'when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O'. The timing is one week, not one month. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: Match each Berlin severity grade with its printed PaO2/FiO2 range — 1) Mild 2) Moderate 3) Severe … A) < 100 B) 100–200 C) 200–300
questions.exp: The severity table reads 'mild — 200 – 300', 'moderate — 100 – 200' and 'severe — < 100'. Lower ratios indicate more severe disease, so the grades run from the highest range to the lowest. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: Which three factors preventing pulmonary edema are printed at the foot of page 233?
opts: Retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells
Lost intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells
Retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and loose junctions between epithelial cells
Retained intravascular protein, blocked interstitial lymphatics, and tight junctions between endothelial cells
questions.exp: The three bullets read 'Retained intravascular protein', 'Interstitial lymphatics drains fluid' and 'Tight junctions between epithelial cells'. ARDS breaks all three, which is why protein-rich fluid floods the alveolus. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: A ventilated patient has ARDS onset three days after a urinary tract infection, bilateral infiltrates, a normal ECHO and PaO2/FiO2 of 150 on PEEP 8 cm H2O. Using the Berlin table, how is this graded and which AECC threshold has changed?
opts: Mild ARDS (200–300); the Berlin definition raises the AECC cut-off from 200 to 300 without grading
Moderate ARDS (100–200); the Berlin definition replaces the single AECC PaO2/FiO2 < 200 cut-off with three graded ranges measured on PEEP ≥ 5 cm H2O
Moderate ARDS (100–200); the Berlin definition removes the PEEP requirement entirely
Severe ARDS (< 100); the Berlin definition is identical to the AECC cut-off of 200
questions.exp: The Berlin severity table reads 'mild 200 – 300', 'moderate 100 – 200' and 'severe < 100', with the brace 'when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O'. The AECC instead used a single 'PaO2/FiO2 < 200' threshold, which is why it captured only about 20% of patients. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed as factors preventing pulmonary edema on page 233, one is not:
opts: Leaky junctions between epithelial cells
Interstitial lymphatics draining fluid
Tight junctions between epithelial cells
Retained intravascular protein
questions.exp: The three protective factors are retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells. Leaky junctions are the pathological change of ARDS, not a protective mechanism. (Book p233)

questions.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
questions.q: Which primary ARDS causes are printed on page 234?
opts: Pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and major burns
Non-pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and post surgery
Pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and post surgery
Pulmonary sepsis, minor blood transfusion, chronic pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and post surgery
questions.exp: The primary list reads 'Pulmonary sepsis', 'massive blood transfusion', 'Acute pancreatitis', 'Transfusion associated lung injury (TRALI)', 'Smoke inhalation', 'Drowning' and 'Post surgery'. Non-pulmonary sepsis and major trauma/burns are the secondary causes printed below it. (Book p234)

questions.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
questions.q: Which secondary ARDS causes are printed on page 234?
opts: Non pulmonary sepsis and massive blood transfusion
Pulmonary sepsis and minor trauma/burns
Non pulmonary sepsis and acute pancreatitis
Non pulmonary sepsis (UTI, surgical site infection) and major trauma/burns
questions.exp: The secondary block reads 'Non pulmonary sepsis (UTI, surgical site infection)' and 'major trauma/burns'. Acute pancreatitis and massive transfusion sit in the primary block above. (Book p234)

questions.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
questions.q: Which mediator sequence does the page 234 pathogenesis diagram print after alveolar epithelial injury?
opts: Inflammatory mediators (IL-2, IL-4, TNF β), cytokines → eosinophil recruitment
Inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-6, TNF α), cytokines → neutrophil recruitment
Inflammatory mediators (IL-10, IL-6, TNF α), cytokines → neutrophil recruitment
Inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-6, TNF α), cytokines → macrophage recruitment only
questions.exp: The vertical chain reads 'Toxin, sepsis → Alveolar epithelial injury → Inflammatory mediators (IL 1, IL 6, TNF α), cytokines → Neutrophil recruitment', alongside a capillary endothelial injury limb feeding exudation. The interleukins are 1 and 6 with TNF alpha. (Book p234)

questions.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
questions.q: Match each consequence of proteinaceous alveolar fluid with its printed label — 1) Loss of surfactant 2) ↓Compliance 3) Impaired gas exchange … A) Collapse B) Impaired gas exchange itself C) Reduced compliance itself
questions.exp: The three arrows from 'Alveolar space proteinaceous fluid + debris' read 'Loss of surfactant → Collapse', '↓Compliance' and 'Impaired gas exchange'. Surfactant loss is the only one with a further downstream arrow, to collapse. (Book p234)

questions.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
questions.q: Which day ranges are printed for the three pathological phases of ARDS?
opts: Acute exudative phase 14 days, fibroproliferative phase 7–14 days, fibrotic vasoconstriction 21–28 days
Acute exudative phase 7 days, fibroproliferative phase 14–21 days, fibrotic vasoconstriction 21–28 days
Acute exudative phase 7 days, fibroproliferative phase 7–14 days, fibrotic vasoconstriction 14–21 days
Acute exudative phase 3 days, fibroproliferative phase 7–14 days, fibrotic vasoconstriction 14–21 days
questions.exp: The phase list reads '1. Acute exudative phase (7 days)', '2. Fibroproliferative phase (7–14 days)' and '3. Fibrotic vasoconstriction (14–21 days)'. The phases overlap rather than following one another cleanly. (Book p234)

questions.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
questions.q: Which finding is called the hallmark of the acute exudative phase, and what alternative name is given?
opts: Neutrophilic hyaline membrane deposition — AKA hyaline membrane disease
Eosinophilic hyaline membrane deposition — AKA diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
Eosinophilic hyaline membrane deposition — AKA hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Eosinophilic hyaline membrane deposition — AKA hyaline membrane disease
questions.exp: The phase 1 entry reads 'Diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) : Interstitial + alveolar edema', then 'Eosinophilic hyaline membrane deposition — Hallmark — a.k.a. hyaline membrane disease.' The membrane is eosinophilic, not neutrophilic. (Book p234)

questions.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the respiratory-failure type printed in the ARDS note on page 234.
opts: False — the note says type 4 respiratory failure is the most common
True — the note says type 1 (most common) or type 3 respiratory failure is seen
False — the note says only type 2 respiratory failure is seen
True — the note says type 2 failure is the most common pattern in ARDS
questions.exp: The note reads 'Type 1 (m/c) or Type 3 respiratory failure seen.' This matches the Type I table on page 230 and the Type III parenchymal row on page 231, where ARDS acts through reduced compliance. (Book p234)

questions.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
questions.q: Which clinical features of ARDS are printed on page 235?
opts: Rapid onset pleuritic pain, hypercarbia, bilateral crackles, bradycardia and pulmonary hypertension
Rapid onset dyspnea, hypoxemia, bilateral crackles with diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, tachypnea/tachycardia/diaphoresis, and pulmonary hypertension from hypoxemic vasoconstriction
Gradual onset dyspnea, hypoxemia, unilateral crackles with a focal infiltrate, bradycardia and systemic hypotension
Rapid onset dyspnea, hypoxemia, bilateral crackles with diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, tachypnea/tachycardia/diaphoresis, and pulmonary hypotension from hypoxemic vasodilatation
questions.exp: The list reads 'Rapid onset dyspnoea', 'Hypoxemia', 'Bilateral crackles : Diffuse pulmonary infiltrates', 'Tachypnoea, tachycardia, diaphoresis' and 'Pulmonary hypertension : D/t hypoxemic vasoconstriction'. The vascular response to hypoxia is vasoconstriction, not vasodilatation. (Book p235)

questions.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
questions.q: Which four mechanical-ventilation strategies are printed as the mainstay of ARDS treatment?
opts: Inverse ratio ventilation with expiration, supine ventilation, permissive hypercapnia, and mechanical ventilation itself as the mainstay
Conventional ratio ventilation, prone ventilation, permissive hypercapnia, and high tidal volume as the mainstay
Inverse ratio ventilation with inspiration, prone ventilation, permissive hypocapnia, and mechanical ventilation itself as the mainstay
Inverse ratio ventilation with inspiration, prone ventilation, permissive hypercapnia, and mechanical ventilation itself as the mainstay
questions.exp: The block reads 'mechanical ventilation : mainstay of treatment', 'Inverse ratio ventilation with inspiration', 'Prone ventilation' and 'Permissive hypercapnia'. Permissive hypercapnia accepts a raised CO2 in exchange for protecting the lung from over-distension. (Book p235)

questions.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
questions.q: Match each form of VILI with its printed pathogenesis — 1) Volume trauma 2) Baro trauma 3) Atelecto trauma … A) Collapse and decollapse during tidal breathing B) ↑Transpulmonary pressure C) ↑Lung volume causing alveolar injury
questions.exp: The table reads 'volume trauma — ↑lung volume → alveolar injury', 'Baro trauma — ↑transpulmonary pressure' and 'Atelecto trauma — Collapse and decollapse during tidal breathing'. Each has its own protective strategy in the next column. (Book p235)

questions.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
questions.q: Match each form of VILI with the protective strategy printed against it — 1) Volume trauma 2) Baro trauma 3) Atelecto trauma … A) High positive end expiratory pressure B) Low tidal volume ventilation (high frequency ventilation) C) Low plateau pressure (low driving pressure)
questions.exp: The treatment column reads 'Low tidal volume ventilation (High frequency ventilation)' for volume trauma, 'Low plateau pressure (low driving pressure)' for baro trauma and 'High positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP)' for atelecto trauma. Each strategy neutralises the specific mechanical stress named beside it. (Book p235)

questions.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
questions.q: Which ventilation settings would the page 235 VILI table pair with a patient showing cyclical alveolar collapse?
opts: Permissive hypercapnia alone, with no change in PEEP
Low plateau pressure, because the mechanism is baro trauma from a raised transpulmonary pressure
High positive end expiratory pressure, because the mechanism is atelecto trauma — collapse and decollapse during tidal breathing
Low tidal volume ventilation, because the mechanism is volume trauma from a raised lung volume
questions.exp: The third row pairs 'Atelecto trauma — Collapse and decollapse during tidal breathing' with 'High positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP)'. PEEP splints open the recruited alveoli and prevents repeated derecruitment. (Book p235)

questions.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
questions.q: Which six-item differential of acute breathlessness closes page 235, and which is marked as the default?
opts: Pulmonary edema (unless proven otherwise), pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, acute exacerbation of asthma, aortic dissection and myocardial infarction
Pulmonary edema (unless proven otherwise), pulmonary embolism, pleural effusion, acute exacerbation of asthma, aortic dissection and myocardial infarction
Pneumonia (unless proven otherwise), pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, acute exacerbation of asthma, aortic dissection and pericarditis
Pulmonary edema (unless proven otherwise), pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, acute exacerbation of COPD, aortic stenosis and myocardial infarction
questions.exp: The note reads 'D/d of acute breathlessness : Pulmonary edema (Unless proven otherwise), Pulmonary embolism, Pneumothorax, Acute exacerbation of asthma, Aortic dissection, myocardial infarction.' Pulmonary oedema heads the list as the default diagnosis, mirroring the ARDS content of the chapter. (Book p235)

units.title: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
units.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
units.guide:
Respiratory failure (p230) is the pulmonary system's inability to meet the body's demands: hypoxemic when PaO2 < 60 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 90%, hypercapnic when PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on room air. The box defines PAO2 as alveolar oxygen, PaO2 as arterial oxygen (normal ~97 mmHg), PaCO2 as arterial carbon dioxide (normal ~40 mmHg) and PAO2 − PaO2 as the alveolocapillary oxygen gradient.
Type I is impaired diffusion causing oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia; pressures are ↓PaO2, normal PaCO2 and ↑PAO2 − PaO2. Causes are interstitial fibrosis/ILD, fluid in the interstitium with pulmonary edema or ARDS, exudate/consolidation in pneumonia, the reduced surface area/volume of emphysema, vascular disease such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis.
Bronchial asthma is entered separately: airway disease with normal parenchyma means absent CO2 retention, so ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↑DLCO, reflecting normal diffusion.

units.title: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
units.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
units.guide:
Type III (p231) runs oxygenation failure → parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure with ↓PaO2, ↑PaCO2 and ↑PAO2 − PaO2; ILD acts by ↓diffusion and ARDS by ↓lung compliance, with the brace showing type 1 becoming type 3 as disease progresses. Type IV is hypotension → ↓perfusion of respiratory muscles with a dash for partial pressures, caused by cardiogenic, hypovolemic or septic shock.
The anaesthesiology 'Type-3' note describes ↓functional residual capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) causing collapse and post-op atelectasis, with causes of supine position/obesity/ascites, residual anaesthesia, upper abdominal incision and airway secretions.
The hypoxemic approach uses V/Q matching: normal 0.8, upper zone > 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q) and lower zone < 1 (dependent). Dead space physiology has ventilation present, perfusion absent and V/Q ∞ (pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vascular disease); shunt physiology has ventilation absent, perfusion present and V/Q zero (intracardiac/vascular shunts).

units.title: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
units.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
units.guide:
The hypoxemic flowchart (p232) starts from ↓PaO2 and branches to V/Q mismatch (Type I, diffusion abnormality), V/Q = 0 shunt and V/Q = ∞ dead space.
It then splits on PaCO2: a raised CO2 with a normal gradient ends in hypoventilation (Type II), and with a raised gradient in hypoventilation plus another mechanism (Type III). Without CO2 retention, a raised gradient with oxygen-correctable hypoxaemia means V/Q mismatch and uncorrectable hypoxaemia means shunt, while a normal gradient leads to high altitude.
The hypercapnic flowchart starts from ↑PaCO2 and splits on the A-a gradient: normal → hypoventilation → generator, pumps, effector organ; increased → V/Q mismatch, eg ARDS and ILD.

units.title: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
units.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
units.guide:
ARDS (p233) is AKA shock lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury. The 1992 AECC criteria are non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema with PCWP < 18 mmHg (the wedge measures left atrial pressure and suggests no cardiac abnormality), bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates on X-ray, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200; only 20% of patients meet them, mortality is 70–75% and post-ARDS residual disability is present.
The Berlin 2012 definition requires acute onset within 1 week of the insult, bilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, a non-cardiogenic cause with normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O — mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe < 100.
Pulmonary edema is prevented by retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells.

units.title: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
units.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
units.guide:
Primary ARDS (p234) follows pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning or post surgery; secondary ARDS follows non-pulmonary sepsis (UTI, surgical site infection) or major trauma/burns.
Pathogenesis: toxin/sepsis → alveolar epithelial injury → inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-6, TNF α) and cytokines → neutrophil recruitment, with capillary endothelial injury causing exudation of fluid and protein; the alveolar space fills with proteinaceous fluid and debris, causing loss of surfactant → collapse, ↓compliance and impaired gas exchange. Type 1 (most common) or type 3 respiratory failure is seen.
Phases: acute exudative phase (7 days) with diffuse alveolar damage, interstitial and alveolar edema and eosinophilic hyaline membrane deposition as the hallmark (AKA hyaline membrane disease); fibroproliferative phase (7–14 days); fibrotic vasoconstriction (14–21 days).

units.title: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
units.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
units.guide:
Clinical features (p235): rapid onset dyspnea, hypoxemia, bilateral crackles with diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, tachypnea, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and pulmonary hypertension from hypoxemic vasoconstriction.
Management is mechanical ventilation as the mainstay, with inverse ratio ventilation with inspiration, prone ventilation and permissive hypercapnia.
VILI: volume trauma (↑lung volume → alveolar injury) is treated with low tidal volume ventilation (high frequency ventilation); baro trauma (↑transpulmonary pressure) with low plateau pressure (low driving pressure); atelecto trauma (collapse and decollapse during tidal breathing) with high PEEP.
The differential of acute breathlessness is pulmonary edema (unless proven otherwise), pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, acute exacerbation of asthma, aortic dissection and myocardial infarction.
